title: Fire loads, heating and electrical ignition
audience: Coordinators, support workers and trained cleaners who may be asked to work in a home affected by hoarding or environmental neglect, as part of an authorised support plan. Not a qualification or authority to clear a property, dispose of a resident's belongings, enter by force, or provide welfare or clinical support.
learningOutcomes: Identify combustible loads near heat sources and electrical points from a safe position.
Stop work and escalate fire-load findings without touching stacks or equipment.
Record the hazard with its location, date and referral.

instruction.heading: Scope of this lesson
instruction.body: This lesson covers recognition and escalation only. It does not authorise work on heaters, electrical wiring, power boards or appliances, and it does not authorise moving stored items away from a heat source without an agreed plan.

instruction.heading: Why accumulated possessions raise the risk
instruction.body: The CFA says that clutter can easily catch fire and increase the intensity of a fire, and that hoarding makes fires more likely to start. Fire Rescue Victoria says hoarding increases the risk of having a fire, and that accumulated possessions create an abnormally high fuel load. Combustible storage near a heat source or an electrical point raises both the chance of ignition and the speed at which a fire spreads. The consequence is greater where escape routes are blocked, which is the subject of the next lesson.

instruction.heading: Recognising ignition points from a safe position
instruction.body: Look for combustible material stacked near heaters, cooking areas, electrical boards, power boards and appliances, for cords running under piles, and for heat sources left among paper. Observe from the doorway or another safe vantage point. Do not touch or move anything, and do not test appliances. Record what you see, with the room and the date. Where a source looks active or the risk looks immediate, leave the area and follow the emergency procedure named in the plan. Fire-risk decisions belong to the competent fire service and to the specialists the plan names, so report the condition to the coordinator the same day and suspend work in the affected rooms until the risk has been assessed.

procedure: Stop in the doorway. Do not enter the pile area to inspect it.
From a safe position, identify heat sources and electrical points, and note the combustible material within reach of each.
Check whether any exit, door or alarm is affected, and record that.
Do not touch appliances, cords or heaters. Do not move material near an ignition point.
Escalate the fire-load finding to the coordinator, and follow the emergency procedure in the plan if the condition looks immediate.
Record what was seen, when and where, and suspend work in the affected rooms until a decision is recorded.

workedExamples.situation: Paper is stacked around a heater, and a door cannot fully open.
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop work in the affected area, escalate the fire and access hazard to the competent service, and do not disturb the stacks. Record the no-touch ignition risk and agree low-disruption steps with the resident.

workedExamples.situation: Extension leads run under a pile of clothes, and a power board sits behind a stack of cardboard.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the boundary for the crew?
workedExamples.reasoning: Record and escalate. Do not move the stack or the leads, and do not repair or test the board. The competent person decides the remedy.

equipmentAndPpe: Hazard log with fields for location, time, ignition source and the material nearby.
Barrier tape and signage for suspended zones.
Training-only photographs or drawings. No real electrical or heating equipment is handled in this lesson.

commonErrors.error: Moving paper away from a heater to tidy up, without a plan.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, record the risk and let the competent service and the agreed plan decide any move.

commonErrors.error: Assuming a fire risk is minor because nothing has burned.
commonErrors.prevention: Recognise that accumulated possessions raise the fuel load, and escalate.

commonErrors.error: Working near an electrical board with stacked material on it.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep out of the zone, record it and escalate.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Fire-risk, heating and electrical matters are restricted to competent people. Completing this lesson does not qualify a worker to work on electrical or heating equipment.
The CFA and Fire Rescue Victoria pages are Victorian guidance. Fire-safety rules in other states and territories were not checked for this lesson.

qualityStandard: The learner identifies combustible loads near heat and electrical points in a described scene, from a safe position.
The learner stops work and escalates without touching stacks or equipment.
The learner records the hazard, the time, the location and the referral.
documentationEvidence: Hazard log entry with location, date and the ignition sources observed.
Referral record to the coordinator or competent service, and any emergency action taken.
Record of suspended work areas and the decision that lifted the suspension.
summary: Accumulated possessions raise the fuel load.
Look from a safe position, and touch nothing near heat or electrical points.
Escalate fire-risk decisions to the competent service.
Risk reduction, not disruption, is the first aim.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which condition most increases the consequence of a fire in a crowded home?
options: Books stored on a bookshelf away from any appliance.
Combustible storage close to a heat source, with escape routes blocked.
A clean floor with no items on it.

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the correct first action when a power board is covered by stacked cardboard?
options: Clear the cardboard so the board can be checked.
Unplug the board and carry on working.
Record and escalate from a safe position, without moving the stack or testing the board.

knowledgeChecks.question: According to Fire Rescue Victoria's hoarding guidance, what is the preferred approach to fire risk?
options: Risk reduction as a priority, rather than large scale removal.
Large scale removal of all possessions as soon as possible.
Leaving the home as it is until the resident asks for help.

officialReferences.title: Hoarding and fire safety (Country Fire Authority, Victoria)
officialReferences.covers: Read through a summary tool on 2026-11-03. The page says clutter can easily catch fire and increase the intensity of a fire; hoarding makes fires more likely to start; hallways, windows and doors can become blocked, so getting in and out is harder; hoarded objects can stop sprinkler water reaching a fire in apartments; one-off clean-ups do not deal with the underlying reasons for hoarding behaviour; and hoarding is a complex issue requiring intervention and long-term support. Publisher: Country Fire Authority (Victoria).

officialReferences.title: Hoarding (Fire Rescue Victoria)
officialReferences.covers: Read through a summary tool on 2026-11-03. The page says FRV firefighters respond to a fire or emergency where there is hoarding or environmental neglect every 4 to 6 days; hoarding increases the risk of having a fire; accumulated possessions result in an abnormally high fuel load; and FRV recommends risk reduction as a priority rather than large scale removal. Publisher: Fire Rescue Victoria.

moduleAuthority.heading: Module authority and restricted work
moduleAuthority.body: This module is training content. It does not grant authority to enter a home by force, to clear, sort or dispose of a resident's belongings without valid consent, to handle or dispose of hazardous waste, to deal with unstable stacks or structural hazards, or to provide welfare, clinical or safeguarding assessments. Completing this lesson does not give a licence, certificate or approval. Work is done only under an authorised support plan and a written agreement with the resident, within the limits set by the employer and the local law. Tenancy, safeguarding and information-sharing rights are jurisdiction-specific, and fire-risk, structural, pest and hazardous-waste decisions belong to the competent authorities and specialists named in the plan. Where authority or consent is unclear, stop and refer.

stopWorkAndReferral.heading: Stop-work and referral rules for this module
stopWorkAndReferral.body: Stop and refer whenever any of these is true: consent is not specific, documented and current; the resident has objected or withdrawn consent; a party seeks entry by force, nonconsensual disposal or removal of personal documents; a fire-load, ignition, egress or obstruction hazard is present; a stack or structure is unstable; pests, unknown liquids or mouldy goods are present; sharps, chemicals or unknown containers are found; waste would go to general disposal without characterisation; private information is requested without authority; or the work would go beyond the approved plan. Stopping is a valid professional outcome. Record the disagreement, protect the resident's choices and refer the authority dispute before any property is moved.
